analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau, 35.5% of educational services firms reported using AI in the last two weeks, up from 33.8% in the prior period. The survey first asked this question in September 2023 and covers NAICS 61, educational services. The figure reflects the share of firms answering yes to a two week recall window, so it captures active, recent use rather than experimental or one time adoption.

The Department of Education's AI inventory shows the range of tasks where the department itself deploys AI. These include writing assistance through Grammarly, meeting and lecture transcription through Otter.AI, and foundation model applications via AWS Bedrock for text generation, summarization, conversational AI, personalization, and content creation. The inventory also lists AI for generating code snippets, extracting key points from documents, producing R code for data analysis, creating mock datasets for testing, drafting outreach strategies and project plans, and suggesting job descriptions and workflow diagrams. CAISY is described as delivering real time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation to reduce costs and boost productivity, though no measured return on investment figures are reported in these excerpts.

The Department of Education has issued federal guidance for schools that frames permissible use, risk, and procurement. The department states it adheres to federal regulations and the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence, and it emphasizes responsible and secure usage. Its inventory includes a use case where AI is given fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information to ensure filters and data loss prevention methods are in place, indicating attention to security controls, but the excerpts do not quantify specific risk outcomes.

HolonIQ tracks the education economy, including EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher education, and workforce learning. The platform describes capabilities for sizing addressable markets, forecasting demand, mapping competitive and partnership landscapes, and supporting buy, build, or partner decisions. However, the excerpt does not report specific vendor shares, dollar totals, or concentration data for AI in education.

The World of AI's course catalog tracks 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, with 3 offering public companion code. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry providers including DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and Andrej Karpathy. The catalog notes that only three courses list an accompanying public code repository, and it does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

A reader deciding whether to deploy AI in education should note that adoption among educational services firms is already above one third and rising, and that federal guidance exists to frame permissible use and risk. At the same time, the sources here do not provide measured ROI evidence or vendor concentration figures, and the course data lacks completion outcomes. The picture is one of established, regulated adoption with clear use cases, but thin public evidence on financial returns and market structure.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
